opus-5.5.text:
I think it ends up looking a lot more like private deployment than people assumed a couple of years ago. Early on, the default was "call an API, send your data to someone's cloud, get a response back." That's great for prototyping, and for a lot of consumer use cases it's fine. But once you get into the enterprises doing the most valuable work, like banks, healthcare systems, governments, and telecoms, the data they want these models to touch is the most sensitive data they have. Customer records, financial transactions, internal IP. They're not going to pipe that out to a third party they don't control.

So what we've seen, and what I think wins long term, is the model coming to the data rather than the data going to the model. That means deploying inside the customer's own VPC, on whichever cloud they've already standardized on, and in some cases fully on-prem or even air-gapped. Being cloud-agnostic matters a lot here, because enterprises don't want to be locked into one hyperscaler just to get access to a model.

The other piece is efficiency. If you're asking a company to run the model on their own hardware, you can't hand them something that needs a massive cluster just to serve it. So there's real pressure to build models that are highly capable but compact enough to deploy economically, maybe on a couple of GPUs. I think that trade-off between capability and deployability is underrated, and it's going to decide who actually gets adopted at scale in the enterprise.

And then on top of that, the deployment model isn't just "where does the model run." It's also how deeply it's customized. The companies getting the most value are fine-tuning on their own data and connecting the model to their internal systems and tools. That only really works when it all lives inside their perimeter. So my bet is private, flexible, customizable deployment becomes the norm for serious enterprise use, and the pure shared-API model is more of an on-ramp than the destination.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that private, flexible deployment will become the norm for enterprise use, but does not state that enterprise generative AI adoption will require support.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that there isn't going to be one winner, and anyone telling you there will be is probably selling you that one option. But if you push me on where the center of gravity ends up, I'd say it's going to be private deployments, where the model runs inside the customer's environment, whether that's their own data center or their VPC on a cloud they already trust.

The reason is pretty simple. The data that makes these models actually useful inside a large enterprise is the data they'd never want to send out the door. It's contracts, it's customer records, it's internal knowledge bases, it's the stuff regulators care about. When we talk to banks, healthcare companies, governments, the first question is never "how smart is the model?" It's "where does my data go?" And if the answer is "to our API," the conversation ends with a lot of these customers before it even starts.

So we've put a lot of effort into being cloud-agnostic and deployable anywhere. Same model on AWS, on Azure, on Oracle, on-prem, air-gapped if you need it. That flexibility is itself the product for a lot of buyers. They don't want to be locked into one hyperscaler's model stack, and they definitely don't want to rebuild their entire data posture around a single vendor's API.

Now, I don't think the API model dies. For startups, for experimentation, for a lot of lower-sensitivity use cases, the API is great. It's fast, it's cheap to get started, you don't have to run anything. And that's a big market. But I think the bulk of the revenue in enterprise, the really serious, large, multi-year deals, is going to be in deployments where the enterprise controls the environment. And the models that win there are going to be the ones that are efficient enough to actually run in those environments at reasonable cost, not just the biggest model you can possibly build.

The other piece is that enterprises don't buy a model, they buy a system. Retrieval, tool use, fine-tuning on their own data, guardrails, all of that has to come with it. So the deployment model that wins is the one that packages all of that in a way that an enterprise can actually own and operate. That's where I think the market goes.

r001.rationale: The response says private deployments will be the long-term center of gravity for enterprise AI and describes support for customer-controlled environments across cloud, on-premises, and air-gapped setups.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s going to be a mix, because enterprises have very different constraints. If you’re building a prototype, calling an API is a great way to get started. But if you’re a bank and you want to use your most sensitive internal data, where the model runs and who can access that data become central questions.

So I’d expect a lot of enterprise adoption to happen inside the customer’s cloud environment, with some deployments on-premises where that’s necessary. You bring the model to the data, and the enterprise keeps control over access and governance.

The winning approach, in my view, is to make that flexibility easy. Customers shouldn’t have to become experts in operating models just to get those guarantees. They want something that fits their infrastructure, performs reliably, and actually makes a workflow better.

r001.rationale: The response expects enterprise adoption to use a mix of deployment models and says customers need flexible support for their infrastructure and governance needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s going to be a mix, because enterprises have very different requirements. For some, consuming a model through an API is exactly what they want: it’s simple, they don’t have to operate the infrastructure, and they can get moving quickly. For others, the data is sensitive enough that the model needs to come to their environment, whether that’s their cloud or on premises.

So I think the winning approach is to give enterprises that flexibility. You shouldn’t have to move your data somewhere you’re uncomfortable with just to use a model. And you shouldn’t have to build an entire infrastructure team if all you need is an API. Ultimately, the deployment model needs to fit the business, and the technology should make that choice easier.

r001.rationale: The response discusses offering API and in-environment deployment options, but does not state that enterprise adoption will require ongoing support in the long term.
